chunks: How EMI shields work. The question: How do EMI shields work?
A metal shield works in two ways. Most of a radio wave bounces off the metal surface, which is reflection.
The small part that gets in dies out inside the metal, because it makes eddy currents (circulating currents in the metal) that oppose it, which is absorption.
Electric fields are easy to block with grounded metal, slow magnetic fields are hard, and real shields are limited by leaks.
Picture a mirror in front of a dark curtain. The mirror bounces most light back. Whatever slips past is soaked up by the curtain. A thin mirror reflects as well as a thick one.
Slow magnetic fields are different: they reflect poorly, and a thin curtain barely absorbs them.
Most of the incident wave reflects at the surface (orange). What enters decays exponentially over skin depths (red), and what emerges (grey) is very small.
The shield's decibels are the sum of the reflected and absorbed fractions.
Reflection: the wave bouncing off the metal because the metal is so unlike air. Absorption: the wave fading as it passes through the metal.
Skin depth: how deep a field goes into a metal before it fades to about a third. It shrinks as frequency rises.
Eddy currents: circulating currents a changing field creates in the metal. Aperture: any gap in a shield, such as a seam or vent, that leaks. Decibel (dB): a way to compare sizes.
20 decibels is a factor of 10 in field strength.
Take a 35 µm copper foil. At 100 megahertz copper's skin depth is 6. 6 µm, so the foil is more than five skin depths thick.
It absorbs about 46 decibels (a factor of about 200), and reflection adds about 88 decibels. At 1 kilohertz the skin depth is 2. 09 mm, so the same foil absorbs only about 0.
15 decibels. Against slow, close magnetic sources use steel, a smaller loop, or distance.
That is the whole idea: reflection plus absorption, strong at radio frequencies, weak for slow magnetic fields.
"A shield works by reflection and absorption.
The metal's surface impedance is milliohms against 377 ohms for a far-field wave, so most of it reflects; what gets in is absorbed because eddy currents oppose it, decaying over a skin depth, 6.
6 microns for copper at 100 megahertz. Electric fields are easy to shield with any grounded conductor.
Low-frequency magnetic fields are hard, because reflection is weak and thin copper absorbs little, so you need high-permeability material or loop control.
And in practice leakage through seams and holes sets the real performance."
